subject: chemistry
title: Organic Chemistry Adventure 3: Mechanisms — SN1 vs SN2
welcome_lead: Today you'll compare SN1 and SN2 reactions — the heart of organic mechanisms.
meta_desc: Chemistry HL — nucleophilic substitution SN1 vs SN2, kinetics, stereochemistry.
final_note: You learned SN1 is two-step (carbocation intermediate), SN2 is one-step (backside attack); SN1 favours 3° + polar protic, SN2 favours 1° + polar aprotic.

walkthroughs.body_html:
One step, concerted: nucleophile attacks back of C as leaving group leaves.

Rate = k[R-X][Nu⁻] (second order).

Stereochemistry: inversion (Walden inversion).

Favoured by: primary halogenoalkanes, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent.

Two steps:
1. Slow: R-X → R⁺ + X⁻ (carbocation forms).
2. Fast: R⁺ + Nu⁻ → R-Nu.

Rate = k[R-X] only (first order).

Stereochemistry: racemic mixture (carbocation planar; attack either side).

Favoured by: tertiary (stable carbocation), polar protic solvent.

Primary halogenoalkanes → almost always SN2.
Tertiary → almost always SN1.
Secondary → either depending on conditions.

Leaving group ability: I > Br > Cl > F (weaker C-X bond).

Solvent polarity: SN1 boosted by polar protic; SN2 boosted by polar aprotic.

Free radical halogenation of alkanes: initiation (UV), propagation (Cl· + RH), termination.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.

mcqs.q: How does the rate of an SN2 reaction depend on concentrations?
options: SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
SN2 reactions are first order overall because only the substrate matters.
Rate is first order in both substrate AND nucleophile (overall second order) because both are involved in the rate-determining step.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
